5. Historical Data Collection

Coastal water levels are measured using tide gauges, which are mechanical measuring devices placed along the shore. These devices measure the change in sea level relative to the land surface. NOAA (2014) describes tide gauge data and how they were collected. Data collection methods are documented in a series of manuals and standards that can be accessed at NOAA’s CO-OPS Publications site. This feature uses hourly averages based on each tide gauge’s continuous measurements.

Observed tide gauge data for this pairing come from NWLON, which comprises 210 long-term, continuously operating tide gauge stations along the U.S. coast, including the Great Lakes and islands in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. This feature shows trends for a subset of stations along the ocean coasts that met certain criteria for sufficient long-term data, as detailed in the technical documentation for the Coastal Flooding indicator. That documentation also explains the rationale for choosing 1950 as a starting point based on overall data availability.

6. Indicator Derivation

This pairing examines the number of days in which a particular location registers water levels that exceed a threshold for “minor flooding” that NOAA has defined at each location. Thus, it captures all flooding events that exceed each location’s threshold, which means it captures floods that may range from small “nuisance” floods to much larger but less frequent major floods. Station-specific flood thresholds for locations presented in this feature, as well as other locations, are listed in Table A1.3 of Sweet et al. (2022). Sweet et al. (2018) and Sweet et al. (2022) explain how NOAA derived each location’s flood thresholds based on a probabilistic examination of historical observations. This pairing excludes certain sites where thresholds were established or updated after 2018—most notably, Alaska and Pacific island stations—because the 2018 projections would have either excluded these stations or applied different thresholds from those that EPA’s observed indicator now uses.

Observed Data

Historical numbers were derived by calculating each day’s maximum water level based on hourly water level data, then comparing these daily maxima with threshold levels for flooding at each tide gauge. The total number of days exceeding the derived flooding threshold was calculated for each tide gauge and for every calendar year. Annual totals were averaged together over multi-year periods.

Projections

The project team obtained source data from NOAA. These data present a projected number of flood days for each year through 2100 at each applicable tide gauge location, for each scenario. The team calculated decadal means and chose two future decades for display, representing mid- and late-century.

7. Alignment

Observed and projected concentrations are closely aligned. NOAA’s 2018 projection data set similarly shows observed and projected numbers on a smooth continuum. No transformation was necessary to improve the alignment.

8. Display

The interactive maps for this pairing show the following elements:

  • Observed data from EPA’s indicator for seven decades, from the 1950s to the 2010s.
  • Projections from the 2020s through to the 2090s for two of NOAA’s sea level scenarios (intermediate-low, labeled “lower sea level rise,” and intermediate, labeled “higher sea level rise”).

Each point on the map shows the number of flood days per year, averaged over 10 years. The map also allows users to open a popup with a column graph for each measurement location. The column graph shows the number of flood days per year, averaged by decade, with side-by-side comparison between the observed record and the two sea level scenarios listed above.

9. Quality Assurance and Quality Control

Quality assurance and quality control procedures for U.S. tide gauge data are described in various publications available at NOAA’s CO-OPS Publications site. For each pairing, the project team conducted typical quality control steps including independently checking all aggregations, unit conversions, transformations, and other calculations.
